title: ‘Exclude all from pensioner health rise’
full_text:
Greens leader David Shoebridge has ruled out supporting Labor’s private health insurance rebate cut for over-65s unless all pensioners are exempt, not just Australians on the full pension, saying “half-measures” will be rejected.
Confirmation that the Greens aren’t open to exempting full pensioners while still seeing part pensioners pay more will force the Albanese government to forgo at least half of the $3bn in savings it wanted to book to help fund aged-care beds and services, as Labor faces increasing pressure to produce net savings in its mid-year budget update and ease inflation.
The Australian reported last month that any government proposal to carve out only full pensioners would have to go through the Greens’ partyroom.
Senator Shoebridge on Wednesday hardened his party against anything but an exemption for all pensioners. “We have been clear for months that we will support the bill if Labor excludes all pensioners from the rebate changes. We won’t consider half-measures when it comes to protecting people who are already doing it tough in a cost-of-living crisis,” he said.
“The Greens will not allow Labor to punch down on pensioners for quick cash, especially at the same time they are refusing to tax gas companies making a killing in war profits. None of the money planned from rolling back the rebate is slated to go into healthcare, and there is no plan for pensioners who are on fixed incomes and structured their lives around this system.
“During an inquiry into this change, we heard from people planning to cut back on essentials like heating, cooling and putting food on the table just to maintain their current level of cover. That is the reality we need to face.” Health Minister Mark Butler has signalled he’s open to a debate in parliament about carving out full pensioners after the Coalition teamed up with the Greens and crossbenchers to discharge the bill from the Senate notice paper last month.
Determined to find savings to “fund the huge expansion that is needed in aged care”, Mr Butler reintroduced an identical piece of legislation the next day.
Labor has 33 bills before parliament with two Senate sitting weeks and one House of Representatives sitting week left before the summer break.
The government’s priorities for the final sitting fortnight include the private health insurance changes, the digital duty of care regime, the domestic gas reservation and a minimum tax on discretionary trusts.
Mr Butler on Wednesday would not say whether the government was willing to exempt all pensioners from having to pay the higher rebate in a bid to clinch a deal with the Greens, or whether he had begun looking for alternative savings to pay for 5000 more aged-care beds.
With the Coalition opposed to the legislation, Mr Butler must win over the Greens if he is to push his bill through parliament. The government estimates about 1.2 million pensioners have private health insurance and would be affected by the reforms, compared to the Parliamentary Budget Office, which says there are 1.5 million older Australians affected.
